title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:10)
hookLine: when I am weak, then I am strong

lines: HE PUTS HIS WEAK POINTS ON DISPLAY.
cards: Paul had critics in Corinth, and he quotes them in his own letter. His letters, they say, are "weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible." Strong on paper, unimpressive in person.
The obvious reply to a review like that is a list of achievements. Paul starts one, then turns it upside down.
Instead of hiding his weak points, he puts them on display: the beatings, the shipwrecks, the sleepless nights, the thorn. Then he writes a line that turns it all around.

teach.b: Here's the line, right after the thorn: "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong."
Notice the word therefore. It follows from yesterday's answer, my strength is made perfect in weakness. Paul isn't saying weakness is good in itself.
It's the place where a strength not his own shows up. Just before: "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Earlier in the same letter there's a picture: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." Clay jars. Cheap, breakable kitchen pottery, holding treasure.
If the jar were gold, you'd admire the jar. Because it's clay, you notice what's inside. This isn't only Paul's private mood.

teach.h: THE WEAK THINGS OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: To the same church he wrote earlier, "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty."
Some readers think of a shepherd boy, fishermen, a carpenter's son: people nobody expected much from. Last, what it does not mean.
It doesn't mean staying in harm, or calling cruelty a blessing, or pretending pain is pleasant. Paul's list is hardship for Christ's sake, not abuse to be endured in silence.
The point is honesty: when you stop pretending to be strong, there's room for help, from God, in Paul's telling, and from people.

how: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness, addiction recovery and hard seasons, and some churches and recovery groups speak openly about weakness and dependence on God and on one another rather than hiding them.

o: a reward that comes from hiding your limits well
the idea that suffering is good in itself
a power not your own, showing up where you're weak

Paul quotes his own critics in his letter

games.q: you're Paul. critics say you're weak and unimpressive in person. how do you answer them?
o: list your achievements and prove them wrong.
games.why: Paul boasts in his infirmities, so that the power of Christ may rest on him: when I am weak, then am I strong.

practice: Name one place where you're not strong right now: patience that runs out, a fear, something you can't do, help you need. Say it plainly, without apologizing, and picture a clay jar in your hands, ordinary and a little chipped.
If you pray, offer the weakness to God and ask for strength that isn't yours; if you don't, notice what it's like to stop pretending.
If someone is harming you, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Strength in weakness. Paul's discovery that when he stopped hiding his limits, a power not his own could rest on him: treasure in clay jars.

orig.note: Greek: weakness, infirmity, the word behind "my strength is made perfect in weakness."

carryVoice: Your line: weak, then strong. The treasure was always in clay jars. See you tomorrow.
